--- title: "Competitive Market
Equilibrium" subtitle: "Lecture 4" author: "Div Bhagia" format: revealjs: theme: [default, ../assets/slides.scss] embed-resources: true filters: - ../assets/section-slides.lua --- # Recap from Last Time --- ## Quick Review: Firm Supply **Profit maximization for a price-taking firm:** $$\max_q \pi = P \cdot q - C(q)$$ **First-order condition:** $P = MC(q)$ **Short-run supply curve:** Portion of the MC curve above AVC **Key insight:** The firm produces where price equals marginal cost, as long as it covers variable costs --- ## From Individual to Market **Last time:** Individual firm decisions — production functions, cost minimization, profit maximization **Today:** How do individual decisions aggregate into market outcomes? - How are market demand and supply constructed? - What determines equilibrium prices? - What happens when conditions change? - Is the competitive outcome efficient? # Market Demand and Supply --- ## Market Demand Individual $i$ has demand: $x_i(p_x, p_y, I_i)$ **Market demand** is the horizontal sum of individual demands: $$X(p_x, p_y, I_1, \ldots, I_m) = \sum_{i=1}^{m} x_i(p_x, p_y, I_i)$$ If each individual's demand is downward sloping, so is market demand **Shifts in market demand:** Changes in income, prices of related goods, preferences, or number of consumers shift the curve --- ## Market Demand: Graphical Construction ::: {#5c9272e0 .cell fig-height='4' fig-width='10' execution_count=1} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](slides4_files/figure-revealjs/cell-2-output-1.png){width=950 height=371 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: At any price, market quantity is the sum of individual quantities demanded --- ## Market Demand Elasticity $$e_{D,P} = \frac{\partial X}{\partial P} \cdot \frac{P}{X}$$ **Classification:** - $|e_{D,P}| > 1$: Elastic demand - $|e_{D,P}| = 1$: Unit elastic - $|e_{D,P}| < 1$: Inelastic demand **Why it matters for equilibrium:** The elasticity of demand determines how market prices respond to supply shocks --- ## Short-Run Market Supply Each firm $j$ has short-run supply $q_j(P, v, w)$ **Market supply** is also a horizontal sum: $$Q^S(P, v, w) = \sum_{j=1}^{n} q_j(P, v, w)$$ Since each firm's supply curve slopes upward (rising MC), market supply also slopes upward **Supply elasticity:** $$e_{S,P} = \frac{\partial Q^S}{\partial P} \cdot \frac{P}{Q^S} > 0$$ --- ## Market Supply: Graphical Construction ::: {#10c5b4e0 .cell fig-height='4' fig-width='10' execution_count=2} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](slides4_files/figure-revealjs/cell-3-output-1.png){width=958 height=372 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: Market supply is the horizontal sum of individual firms' supply (MC) curves # Short-Run Equilibrium --- ## Equilibrium Price Determination An **equilibrium price** $P^*$ solves: $$Q^D(P^*) = Q^S(P^*)$$ The equilibrium price serves two functions: - **Signal to producers:** How much to produce - **Rationing device:** Allocates goods among consumers At $P^*$, neither demanders nor suppliers have an incentive to change behavior --- ## Short-Run Equilibrium: The Big Picture ::: {#fb6a7ec0 .cell fig-height='4' fig-width='10' execution_count=3} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](slides4_files/figure-revealjs/cell-4-output-1.png){width=950 height=371 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: Once price is determined in the market, each firm and individual takes this price as given --- ## Timing of the Supply Response How quickly can supply adjust to a demand shift? **Very short run:** Quantity is fixed — price does all the adjusting **Short run:** Existing firms adjust output but no entry/exit **Long run:** Firms can enter or exit, all inputs are variable The distinction matters enormously for policy analysis — the time horizon determines who bears the burden of a shock --- ## Very Short Run: Fixed Supply ::: {#24083198 .cell fig-height='4.5' fig-width='6' execution_count=4} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](slides4_files/figure-revealjs/cell-5-output-1.png){width=571 height=420 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: When supply is perfectly inelastic, price acts purely as a rationing device --- ## Application: Concert Tickets and Surge Pricing **Very short run in action:** - Concert venues have fixed capacity (vertical supply) - A surge in demand → prices must rise to ration seats - Explains why popular concerts sell out / prices spike on resale markets **Uber/Lyft surge pricing** works similarly: in the very short run, the number of drivers is nearly fixed, so price surges ration available rides **Question:** Is this "fair"? We'll return to welfare analysis shortly # Comparative Statics --- ## Shifts in Supply and Demand | Demand Curves Shift Because | Supply Curves Shift Because | |:----|:----| | Incomes change | Input prices change | | Prices of substitutes/complements change | Technology changes | | Preferences change | Number of producers changes | **Key insight:** The relative magnitudes of price and quantity changes depend on the shapes (elasticities) of the curves --- ## Effect of a Supply Shift: Role of Demand Elasticity ::: {#40b6ea4b .cell fig-height='4.5' fig-width='10' execution_count=5} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](slides4_files/figure-revealjs/cell-6-output-1.png){width=950 height=419 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: Elastic demand → quantity adjusts more, price less. Inelastic demand → price absorbs most of the shock. --- ## A Comparative Statics Model **Demand:** $Q^D = D(P, \alpha)$ where $\alpha$ shifts demand **Supply:** $Q^S = S(P, \beta)$ where $\beta$ shifts supply **Equilibrium:** $D(P^*, \alpha) = S(P^*, \beta)$ Differentiate with respect to $\alpha$: $$D_P \frac{dP^*}{d\alpha} + D_\alpha = S_P \frac{dP^*}{d\alpha}$$ $$\frac{dP^*}{d\alpha} = \frac{D_\alpha}{S_P - D_P} > 0$$ Since $D_P < 0$, $S_P > 0$, and $D_\alpha > 0$ (demand increase), equilibrium price rises --- ## In Elasticity Form $$\frac{dP^*/P^*}{d\alpha} = \frac{e_{D,\alpha}}{e_{S,P} - e_{D,P}}$$ $$\frac{dQ^*/Q^*}{d\alpha} = \frac{e_{S,P} \cdot e_{D,\alpha}}{e_{S,P} - e_{D,P}}$$ **Intuition:** If supply is elastic ($e_{S,P}$ large), quantity adjusts more and price adjusts less. The reverse with inelastic supply. This is the workhorse framework for policy analysis — any shock to demand or supply can be traced through these expressions --- ## Application: Agricultural Price Volatility **Why do agricultural prices fluctuate so much?** Supply shifts (weather, disease) combined with: - **Inelastic demand** for food (people need to eat) - **Inelastic short-run supply** (crops already planted) Result: Supply shocks cause large price swings **Policy responses:** Price supports, crop insurance, strategic reserves — all attempt to stabilize prices, but each has efficiency costs # Long-Run Equilibrium --- ## Key Assumptions for the Long Run **Entry and exit are free:** No barriers, no special costs **All inputs are variable:** Firms can adjust capital, labor, everything **Firms are identical:** Same cost functions, no special resources **Long-run equilibrium requires:** - $P = MC$ (profit maximization) - $P = AC$ (zero economic profit) - Each firm operates at the minimum of long-run AC --- ## Why Zero Profits? If $P > AC$: Economic profits attract entry → supply shifts right → price falls If $P < AC$: Losses cause exit → supply shifts left → price rises **Process continues until** $P = \min AC$ and economic profits are exactly zero **Remember:** Zero economic profit $\neq$ zero accounting profit. Firms still earn a normal return on invested capital — they just don't earn above-normal returns. --- ## Long-Run Equilibrium: Constant Cost Case ::: {#0f796ea3 .cell fig-height='4.5' fig-width='10' execution_count=6} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](slides4_files/figure-revealjs/cell-7-output-1.png){width=958 height=419 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: With constant costs, the long-run supply curve ($LS$) is perfectly elastic — demand shifts change only the number of firms, not the price --- ## Shape of the Long-Run Supply Curve The long-run supply curve depends on what happens to costs as firms enter: **Constant cost industry:** Entry doesn't affect input prices → $LS$ is horizontal **Increasing cost industry:** Entry bids up input prices → $LS$ slopes upward **Decreasing cost industry:** Entry lowers costs (agglomeration, thicker labor markets) → $LS$ slopes downward --- ## Increasing Cost Industry **Why might entry increase costs?** - New and existing firms compete for scarce inputs (specialized labor, raw materials) - Expansion may impose external costs (congestion, environmental) - Growing demand for tax-financed services **Result:** Long-run equilibrium price rises with industry output **Example:** Housing construction in a growing city — as more homes are built, land prices and construction labor costs are bid up --- ## Decreasing Cost Industry **Why might entry decrease costs?** - Larger pool of trained labor (thicker labor markets) - Critical mass of industrialization enables specialized suppliers - Better transportation and communication networks **Example:** Silicon Valley — clustering of tech firms reduced costs for all through knowledge spillovers, specialized suppliers, and deep labor pools **Result:** Long-run supply slopes downward — expansion makes production cheaper --- ## Application: Why Are Some Industries Concentrated Geographically? **Decreasing cost dynamics help explain industry clusters:** - Finance in New York and London - Tech in Silicon Valley and Seattle - Film in Hollywood - Fashion in Milan and Paris Once a cluster reaches critical mass, the cost advantages attract more firms, reinforcing the agglomeration — a positive feedback loop This connects to Marshall's (1890) three sources of agglomeration economies: input sharing, labor pooling, and knowledge spillovers # Producer Surplus and Rents --- ## Producer Surplus in the Long Run **Producer surplus:** Area below market price and above supply curve - In the **constant cost** case: long-run supply is horizontal → producer surplus is zero - In the **increasing cost** case: supply slopes upward → positive producer surplus **Key question:** Who captures these rents? Must look at the input markets to find the ultimate beneficiaries. --- ## Ricardian Rent **David Ricardo's insight (1817):** Land of varying fertility - At low prices, only the most fertile land is farmed - As demand grows, less fertile (higher cost) land is brought into production - Owners of the most fertile land earn **rents** — returns above what's needed to keep their land in production The long-run supply curve slopes upward because of these differences in costs across producers --- ## Ricardian Rent: Graphical Intuition ::: {#53de334a .cell fig-height='4' fig-width='10' execution_count=7} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](slides4_files/figure-revealjs/cell-8-output-1.png){width=950 height=371 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: Low-cost firms earn Ricardian rents. The marginal firm earns zero profit. Producer surplus in the market measures the sum of all rents. --- ## Capitalization of Rents In practice, Ricardian rents get **capitalized into input prices** - More fertile farmland sells at higher prices - Well-located commercial real estate commands higher rents - Experienced workers in high-demand fields earn wage premiums **Implication:** Once rents are capitalized, even low-cost firms may appear to earn zero economic profit — the "advantage" is reflected in the price they paid for the input # Welfare Analysis --- ## Consumer and Producer Surplus ::: {#124f4865 .cell fig-height='5' fig-width='6' execution_count=8} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](slides4_files/figure-revealjs/cell-9-output-1.png){width=569 height=468 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: **Total surplus** = CS + PS is maximized at the competitive equilibrium --- ## Why Competitive Equilibrium Maximizes Surplus The social planner's problem: choose $Q$ to maximize $$W(Q) = \underbrace{\int_0^Q D(q) \, dq}_{\text{Total value to consumers}} - \underbrace{\int_0^Q S(q) \, dq}_{\text{Total cost of production}}$$ First-order condition: $D(Q^*) = S(Q^*)$ — exactly the competitive equilibrium condition! **Competitive markets get it right:** Decentralized decisions by price-taking agents maximize total surplus --- ## Deadweight Loss Any departure from the competitive outcome creates **deadweight loss** (DWL) — surplus that is lost and captured by no one ::: {#70e0827b .cell fig-height='5' fig-width='6' execution_count=9} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](slides4_files/figure-revealjs/cell-10-output-1.png){width=566 height=468 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: At $Q_1 < Q^*$, the value to consumers (demand) exceeds cost of production (supply) — there are gains from trade being left on the table # Policy Applications --- ## Price Controls and Shortages Setting a price ceiling below equilibrium: - Creates a **shortage**: $Q^D > Q^S$ at the controlled price - **Transfer** from producers to consumers who get to buy at the lower price - **Deadweight loss** from forgone transactions **Example:** Rent control — tenants who find apartments benefit, but some units are withdrawn from the market and some potential renters can't find housing --- ## Price Controls: The Tradeoff ::: {#4ae39170 .cell fig-height='5' fig-width='7' execution_count=10} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](slides4_files/figure-revealjs/cell-11-output-1.png){width=662 height=468 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: Price controls create both a transfer and a deadweight loss --- ## Tax Incidence A per-unit tax $t$ creates a wedge between what buyers pay and sellers receive: $$P^D = P^S + t$$ **Who bears the tax?** Depends on relative elasticities: $$\frac{dP^D/dt}{dP^S/dt} = -\frac{e_{S,P}}{e_{D,P}}$$ **Rule of thumb:** The more inelastic side of the market bears more of the tax - If demand is inelastic (necessities) → consumers bear most of the tax - If supply is inelastic (fixed factors) → producers bear most of the tax --- ## Tax Incidence: Two Cases ::: {#057ad1ef .cell fig-height='4.5' fig-width='10' execution_count=11} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](slides4_files/figure-revealjs/cell-12-output-1.png){width=950 height=420 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: The statutory incidence (who writes the check) doesn't matter — the economic incidence (who bears the burden) is determined by elasticities --- ## Deadweight Loss of Taxation All non-lump-sum taxes involve deadweight losses. A linear approximation: $$DWL \approx -\frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{e_{S,P} \cdot e_{D,P}}{e_{S,P} - e_{D,P}} \cdot \frac{t^2}{P} \cdot Q$$ **Three key insights:** - DWL is proportional to the **square** of the tax rate — doubling the tax more than doubles the welfare cost - Higher elasticities → larger DWL (more behavioral distortion) - Efficient taxation: spread taxes across many goods with low rates rather than taxing one good heavily (Ramsey rule intuition) --- ## Application: Who Pays the Payroll Tax? The U.S. payroll tax (Social Security + Medicare) is nominally split 50-50 between employers and employees **But economic incidence depends on labor supply elasticity:** - Labor supply is relatively inelastic (people need to work) - So workers bear most of the tax, regardless of the statutory split - Employer's "share" is largely passed through as lower wages **Empirical evidence** (Gruber 1997, Saez et al. 2012) confirms: the incidence falls primarily on workers --- ## Try It Yourself Suppose the market for coffee is characterized by: - Demand: $Q^D = 100 - 2P$ - Supply: $Q^S = 3P - 20$ 1. Find the equilibrium price and quantity 2. Calculate consumer surplus and producer surplus 3. If the government imposes a \$5 per-unit tax, find the new equilibrium. How much of the tax do consumers pay? How much do producers pay? 4. Calculate the deadweight loss from the tax # Summary --- ## Key Takeaways **Market equilibrium:** - Market demand and supply are horizontal sums of individual curves - Equilibrium price clears the market and serves as both signal and rationing device - The time horizon (very short, short, long run) determines the supply response **Long-run equilibrium:** - Free entry drives economic profits to zero - Long-run supply depends on how entry affects input costs - Ricardian rents accrue to owners of scarce, low-cost inputs --- ## Key Takeaways (cont.) **Welfare analysis:** - Competitive equilibrium maximizes total surplus (CS + PS) - Price controls and taxes create deadweight losses - Tax incidence depends on relative elasticities, not statutory burden - DWL rises with the square of the tax rate **Limitation:** All of this is partial equilibrium — what happens in one market, holding others constant. Next time we'll consider what happens when everything is connected. --- ## Next Time **Lecture 5: Welfare Analysis and Efficiency** - General equilibrium: why partial equilibrium isn't enough - Production possibilities and the Edgeworth box - The welfare theorems - Applications: trade, environment, redistribution **Reading:** Chapter 13
